summary: Describes how to represent identity information in the RSVP POLICY_DATA object to support policy-based admission control, so a user and application can be securely identified.

plainLanguage.summary: It puts a name tag on a request so the network knows who is asking.

questions: how does rsvp carry user identity
what is the rsvp policy locator
how does kerberos work with rsvp
subtitle: How RSVP messages carry a verifiable user or application identity so routers can apply policy to reservations.

tldr.problem: RSVP reservations are granted under admission control, and policy rules based on who is asking (a user or an application) need that identity to be carried in the RSVP message and verified.
tldr.mechanism: An AUTH_DATA policy element inside the POLICY_DATA object holds a list of typed authentication attributes: a policy locator (a Distinguished Name), a credential such as a Kerberos ticket or X.509 certificate, and optionally a digital signature.
tldr.outcome: Routers and policy decision points can authenticate the requester and admit or reject the reservation, with a POLICY_ERROR attribute explaining failures. It obsoletes RFC 2752, correcting a P-Type codepoint error and a field size error.

today: RFC 3182 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2752, correcting an RSVP POLICY_DATA P-Type codepoint assignment error and a field size error in ErrorValue. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs Identity
sections.content:
RSVP (see RFC 2205) lets a host ask the network for a specific quality of service for a data flow, and routers along the path reserve resources. Permission to reserve depends on two things: whether the resources are available, and whether policy rules are satisfied. Admission control based on user identity or application is described as one of the prime requirements.

To do that, the network must know which user or application is making the request. This RFC defines how to send that identification in RSVP messages (PATH or RESV) so that authorization decisions can use both policy and identity.

The mechanism is the AUTH_DATA policy element, carried inside the POLICY_DATA object. A user process produces it and gives it to the RSVP service on the originating host, which inserts it into the message. Network elements authenticate the request using the credentials in it. After authentication, the first hop router installs the RSVP state and forwards the new policy element returned by the Policy Decision Point (PDP).
sections.plainLanguage: The network wants to know who is asking for a special lane before it hands one out. So the request carries an ID card that routers can check.

sections.title: The AUTH_DATA Policy Element
sections.content:
The AUTH_DATA policy element has a Length field, a P-Type field that says what kind of identity it holds, and then a list of authentication attributes. Length counts the whole element in octets, including the Length and P-Type fields, and MUST be a multiple of 4. The P-Type values start with two entries in the IANA registry: 2 for AUTH_USER (identify users) and 3 for AUTH_APP (identify applications).

Each attribute has a two-octet Length, a one-octet A-Type, a one-octet SubType and a value. Attributes MUST be encoded as a multiple of 4 octets, so shorter ones are padded to a 4-octet boundary. The Length field gives the actual length and does not include the padding.

The A-Type values defined are POLICY_LOCATOR (1), CREDENTIAL (2), DIGITAL_SIGNATURE (3) and POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT (4).
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag is a small box with labelled slots: who you are, proof of who you are, and a signature. Every slot is padded so it lines up neatly in groups of four.

sections.title: The Four Attribute Types
sections.content:
POLICY_LOCATOR holds a unique string, a Distinguished Name (DN), used to find the admission policy for the user or application. Its sub types are ASCII_DN (1) and UNICODE_DN (2) for X.500 DNs as described in RFC 1779, and ASCII_DN_ENCRYPT (3) and UNICODE_DN_ENCRYPT (4) for encrypted DNs, using the Kerberos session key or the digital certificate private key.

CREDENTIAL carries the proof of identity. Sub types are ASCII_ID (1), UNICODE_ID (2), KERBEROS_TKT (3), X509_V3_CERT (4) and PGP_CERT (5).

DIGITAL_SIGNATURE MUST be the last attribute in the list. It signs all data in the policy element up to the signature, using an algorithm that depends on the CREDENTIAL SubType. No sub types are defined, so SubType MUST be 0.

POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT reports failures (see the error section below). The text of the RFC also calls it POLICY_ERROR_CODE in places.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of slots: where to look up your rules, your proof of identity, your signature, and a note saying what went wrong if your request is refused.

sections.title: Authentication Methods
sections.content:
The RFC shows how the attributes are combined for each kind of authentication.

Simple user authentication sends the login ID, as plain ASCII or Unicode text, in a CREDENTIAL attribute (ASCII_ID), next to the user's DN as the policy locator. The RFC notes that simple authentication does not contain a credential that can be securely authenticated and is inherently less secure.

Kerberos puts a Kerberos ticket in the CREDENTIAL attribute (KERBEROS_TKT). It assumes a Key Distribution Center (KDC) is present and that both the host and the verifier (router or PDP) implement Kerberos. In the operational setting, the user application contacts the KDC for a ticket for the next network node or its PDP, sends the ticket in the RSVP message, and the KDC is used to validate it.

Public key authentication puts a digital certificate in CREDENTIAL and adds a DIGITAL_SIGNATURE attribute. The requester signs with its private key. The router or PDP checks the certificate was issued by a trusted certificate authority and verifies the signature with the public key in the certificate.

Application authentication uses P-Type AUTH_APP, with an application identity such as an executable filename (the RFC's example is vic.exe) as an ASCII or Unicode credential.
sections.plainLanguage: You can prove who you are with just your name, with a ticket from a trusted office, or with a stamped certificate plus your own signature. The signature is the hardest to fake.

sections.title: Generating and Processing Identities
sections.content:
Network nodes build AUTH_DATA elements when making a request or forwarding an RSVP message. For user elements, the rules differ by session type. For unicast sessions the user policy locator is copied from the previous hop, while the credentials are those of the current node. For multicast messages, both the policy locator and the credentials are those of the current network node.

For application elements, unicast sessions copy the element from the previous hop. For multicast messages the element is either the first application AUTH_DATA in the message or one chosen by the PDP.

An RSVP host builds a message as in RFC 2205 with changes: the message MAY contain several AUTH_DATA elements, the DN goes in as POLICY_LOCATOR, credentials go in as CREDENTIAL, and if no INTEGRITY object is computed for the message then one SHOULD be computed for the POLICY_DATA object.

A router that is not policy aware SHOULD send the message to the PDP and wait for a response, and rejects the message if the answer is negative. A router that is policy unaware ignores policy data objects and continues. The router or PDP then checks that the identity type is supported and verifies the credential according to the method used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router along the way checks the name tag. If a router has no idea what a name tag is, it just lets the request pass. If it knows, it asks a policy helper whether to say yes.

sections.title: Error Signaling
sections.content:
If the PDP cannot verify an AUTH_DATA element, it MUST return a policy control failure (Error Code = 02) to the policy enforcement point. It SHOULD also supply a policy data object holding an AUTH_DATA element with a policy error attribute that gives more detail. The enforcement point includes that object in the outgoing RSVP error message (PATH_ERROR or RESV_ERROR). Requests themselves SHOULD NOT carry this attribute; it is only inserted into error messages.

The attribute has a 16-bit ErrorValue and an optional OctetString that may hold, for example, a human-readable ASCII message. Its Length MUST be at least 8.
sections.plainLanguage: If your name tag does not pass the check, the answer comes back with a short note saying why, such as that it ran out of time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RSVP INTEGRITY object protects the policy object that carries the identity from attacks, including replay. Combining AUTH_DATA with INTEGRITY gives access control based on both the identity of the user and the identity of the originating node.

The RFC ranks the methods: simple authentication is inherently less secure, Kerberos is reasonably well secured, and public key certificates are known to provide the strongest security.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag you wrote yourself is easy to fake. A ticket from a trusted office is better. A certificate with your signature is best.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Standard policy element types are assigned by IETF Consensus. For A-Types, sub types and the ErrorValue field, the low ranges are allocated through IETF Consensus and the high ranges are reserved for Private Use and not assigned by IANA: A-Type, POLICY_LOCATOR SubType and CREDENTIAL SubType use 0-127 and 128-255, and ErrorValue uses 0-32767 and 32768-65535.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers are handed out by a registry. Some are kept free for people to use privately.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Actual attribute length in octets, excluding padding.

fields.name: A-Type
fields.desc: Attribute type, such as POLICY_LOCATOR or CREDENTIAL.

items.label: ASCII_ID
items.desc: User or application ID as plain ASCII text.

items.label: UNICODE_ID
items.desc: User or application ID as plain Unicode text.

items.label: UNSUPPORTED_CREDENTIAL_TYPE
items.desc: This type of credentials is not supported.

items.label: INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES
items.desc: The credentials do not have sufficient privilege.
